newsitem.title: GERMANY: German, Polish troops fight swollen rivers.
newsitem.headline: German, Polish troops fight swollen rivers.

text.p: Thousands of troops toiled in flood-hit east Germany on Thursday to shore up the banks of the Oder River in the German army's biggest peacetime operation since World War Two.
New surges of high water coursed along the same waterway in Poland, where the death toll from the disaster stands at 55, and officials said weakened dikes could break at any place or time.
In the Czech Republic, church bells rang and sirens blared for a minute at noon to commemorate that country's 49 flood victims to date.
Torrential downpours across central Europe have unleashed the region's worst natural disaster for centuries, and the damage to crops, livestock, property and infrastructure is still being counted.
German officials warned 19,000 residents in the low-lying area of Oderbruch, north of Frankfurt an der Oder, to be ready for evacuation if more dikes reinforcing the banks burst.

Defence Minister Volker Ruehe and Interior Minister Manfred Kanther, visiting the area bordering Poland, said the operation was a "challenge for all Germans" and a token of solidarity between the impoverished east and the more affluent west of Germany.
But officials said that despite the efforts of 8,300 soldiers and 600 border guards, water levels were rising steadily and could unleash more flooding.

Germany has so far escaped the worst of the calamity, but some towns have been hit by power cuts and overflowing sewers. About 500 people have been ordered to leave parts of the danger zone, and farmers have started moving out thousands of head of livestock.
Officials said the situation remained critical, and experts expected a new high point in water levels to be reached about midnight.
Bonn has pledged to help the stricken area in every way possible and has earmarked a 200-million-mark ($110 million) reconstruction fund once the catastrophe is over.

In Brussels, the European Union's executive Commission said it was granting more than 65 million European currency units ($70 million) in aid to Poland, and asking the European Investment Bank to consider loans to the region.
"We want to react quickly to a human disaster," External Affairs Commissioner Hans van den Broek said. He added that he had ordered Commission staff to look for funds to help the Czech Republic.
Polish troops, firemen and volunteers were waiting at key points to repair any flaws in flood defences.

Vast expanses of Polish land were still submerged, delaying clean-up and reconstruction efforts. Camera images from flooded areas showed people taking boats to feed stranded surviving farm animals, wearing masks to bury heaps of bloated pig carcasses or sitting hopelessly on smashed furniture that represented the lost efforts of a lifetime.
In Rybnik in Silesia, troops were gathering corpses washed out of a ravaged cemetery for reburial in a mass grave.

Where waters receded, sewage-laden filth and a lack of clean drinking water threatened dysentery and food-poisoning. Despite such horrors, weather forecasts gave grounds to hope the nearly three-week ordeal was approaching an end.

The billions of dollars worth of damage have raised economic concerns. The zloty currency slipped in Thursday trading and the central bank had to sell dollars to prop it up against speculative selling by Polish banks.

The opposition, grouped around the Solidarity trade union, said the leftist government should issue special bonds to raise flood-relief funds. It renewed calls for a September general election to be postponed while the country recovers from the disaster.

Czechs also face a massive and costly clean-up after the floods destroyed more than 2,000 homes and severed road, rail and telecommunications links. Neighbouring Slovakia said it was cutting its estimate of this year's wheat harvest because of rain damage to crops.
